title: Kidnapped By Danger

jokes.text: The full title read aloud: 'Kidnapped by Danger, colon, The Avery Jessup Story, comma, brought to you with limited commercial interruptions by Pride Bladder Control Pads. Pride: Make Every Room a Bathroom.'
jokes.setup: Liz reads out what seems like a standard TV movie title
jokes.punchline: The title keeps going with a sponsor tagline that reframes every room as a toilet — a deeply undignified product attached to a prestige love story
jokes.explanation: The gag works on multiple levels: the absurd length of the title, the bathos of pairing a romantic kidnapping narrative with bladder control ads, and the tagline's cheerful nihilism ('make every room a bathroom'). The structure is excellent — the comedy escalates as the title keeps going past where you expect it to stop. High quotability and rewatch value because it's dense with comedic information.

jokes.text: Jack's summary of the love story: 'Boy meets girl. Girl gets kidnapped by asian dictator. Boy makes movie to get girl back. Girl's so grateful she does birthday things to boy. Boy falls asleep.'
jokes.setup: Jack frames the movie as 'a classic love story' in the fairy-tale boy-meets-girl structure
jokes.punchline: Each beat escalates absurdity (kidnapping by dictator, 'birthday things'), then deflates with 'boy falls asleep' — a perfectly anticlimactic ending that also characterizes Jack
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's best jokes. The fairy-tale framing ('boy meets girl') applied to increasingly insane real events is structurally brilliant. 'Birthday things' is a perfect euphemism that says everything while saying nothing, and 'boy falls asleep' is a devastatingly funny anticlimax that doubles as sharp character work — Jack's combination of romantic grandiosity and self-serving pragmatism compressed into one beat. High economy, perfectly in character, and very quotable.

jokes.text: Liz: 'You're forgetting boy meets girl's mother. They are creepily attracted to each other.'
jokes.setup: Jack has just presented his sanitized, romantic version of events
jokes.punchline: Liz bluntly inserts the taboo subplot he's conveniently left out
jokes.explanation: A strong setup-deflation beat. The word 'creepily' does a lot of work — it's Liz's editorial judgment delivered flatly, which is very on-brand. Sets up the Diana/Jack tension that drives the episode. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Jack: 'If you get this right, gay men will be dressing up like Avery for Halloween the next 20 years.'
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining why the movie matters to him
jokes.punchline: His metric for success is specifically gay men doing Halloween drag of his wife — oddly specific and weirdly sincere
jokes.explanation: Very Jack — the specificity of the benchmark (gay Halloween drag, 20 years) reveals his peculiar value system and obsession with legacy. The joke is funny because it's a non-sequitur metric that Jack delivers with complete earnestness. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Liz: ''Cause I'm gonna be Mitt Rom-mummy. I call it. You can't steal it.' / Jack: 'Why wouldn't you be Mitt-zombie?' / Liz: 'Because I'm an idiot! Oh, come on, Liz. Think for, like, one second before you buy all that gauze.'
jokes.setup: Liz proudly announces her Halloween costume concept as a portmanteau pun
jokes.punchline: Jack immediately sees the more obvious/better pun; Liz's instant self-flagellation ('Because I'm an idiot!') is the real punchline — she's already bought the gauze
jokes.explanation: A compact comedic gem. The setup is Liz's misplaced pride in a slightly inferior pun; the turn is Jack immediately offering the better version; and the payoff is Liz turning on herself in real time before catching herself talking in third person. 'Before you buy all that gauze' is the capper that implies she's already committed — great specificity. Very Liz, very quotable, tight structure.

jokes.text: Jenna's manager is named 'Gary Greasy' — mentioned deadpan in exposition.
jokes.setup: Jenna explains she has a manager
jokes.punchline: His name is Gary Greasy — a Dickensian joke name delivered without irony
jokes.explanation: A low-key name gag. 'Gary Greasy' is funny in its self-evident sleaziness — the name tells you everything about the character without any elaboration. The payoff gets better retroactively when we learn he's a meth addict.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'I need to thank my co-writers, Gary Greasy and Jesus, a homeless man I stole the melody from.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is in her mind at the awards podium, thanking collaborators
jokes.punchline: She acknowledges stealing from a homeless man named Jesus in her imaginary acceptance speech — the honesty is the joke, as is the casual admission of theft
jokes.explanation: The joke has multiple moving parts: Gary Greasy as a real co-writer name, the name 'Jesus' as a homeless man (not THE Jesus, but ambiguous enough), and the breezy admission of theft. Very Jenna — she'd include him in the credits for plausible deniability while giving herself away completely.

jokes.text: The Weird Al parody reveal: Tracy plays a Weird Al parody of Jenna's 'Kidnapped' song called 'Knapsack' — about a broken zipper and a lost Bakugan toy.
jokes.setup: Jenna has just performed her heartfelt song 'Kidnapped' about her film. Tracy says 'Weird Al' and plays a version
jokes.punchline: The parody is about a broken knapsack and a Bakugan — the mundane specificity of 'lost my Bakugan' vs. the sweeping romantic original is the comedic pivot
jokes.explanation: The bit is structurally clever: the audience hears Jenna's earnest song, then immediately hears the deflating parody version about lost school supplies. 'Bakugan' is a precise, funny choice — it's specific to a child's world and tonally absurd against the romantic backdrop. The scene also escalates into a larger plot about Jenna trying to write a Weird-Al-proof song, which is great absurdist premise-building.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'It's a huge honor. Like, when people wanna see your boobs at Mardi Gras.' / Jenna: 'It's nothing like that.'
jokes.setup: Tracy is trying to console Jenna about the Weird Al parody being an honor
jokes.punchline: Tracy's analogy completely breaks down — being shown at Mardi Gras is not analogous to being parodied by Weird Al in any meaningful way, and Jenna's flat 'it's nothing like that' acknowledges it
jokes.explanation: Tracy's logic is characteristically unhinged — the comparison isn't wrong in spirit (public appreciation) but is so wildly off in register that it reveals his worldview. Jenna's rebuttal is appropriately flat. Reliable Tracy material.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'Weird Al corrupted something beautiful that was written to distract Gary Greasy while he came down from meth.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is defending the artistic integrity of her song
jokes.punchline: The song's true origin — written to occupy a meth-addled manager — retroactively destroys the 'something beautiful' framing
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. It perfectly subverts Jenna's artistic pretension by revealing the completely mercenary and chaotic origin of the song. 'Something beautiful that was written to distract Gary Greasy while he came down from meth' — the construction is immaculate. 'Came down from meth' is the killer phrase, delivered as if it's a perfectly reasonable creative circumstance. It's also a callback to Gary Greasy that pays off the earlier joke with a second, much bigger laugh. Very Jenna.

jokes.text: Kenneth: 'My father wore this to his high school prom. The theme was Enchantment Under the Jim Crow Laws.'
jokes.setup: Someone compliments Kenneth on his tuxedo
jokes.punchline: The reveal that the tux's provenance is a segregation-era prom — delivered with complete guilelessness by Kenneth — is a punch of dark historical comedy
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. It works on several levels simultaneously: Kenneth's rural Southern background and possible supernatural age are both confirmed; the prom theme name is a perfect parody of 'Enchantment Under the Sea'-style prom themes applied to a horrifying historical reality; and Kenneth delivers it with zero awareness that it's troubling. The economy is perfect — just the punchline, no explanation needed. One of the episode's standout moments.

jokes.text: Kenneth: 'But if anything comes up, put a message in a bottle and throw it in the river. That's where I go every day to fish for shoes.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth has been told there are no job openings
jokes.punchline: His preferred communication method and daily activity — fishing for shoes in a river — reveals a poverty/lifestyle so specific and absurd it becomes surreal character comedy
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Kenneth joke. 'Fish for shoes' is the kind of specific absurdist detail that defines 30 Rock at its best — it simultaneously implies his poverty, his rural background, his cheerful acceptance of deprivation, and his complete obliviousness to how strange this sounds. Delivered with Kenneth's standard guileless sincerity. Very quotable and one of the episode's most memorable lines.

jokes.text: The old janitor's advice: 'Throw your resume away on the fourth floor and we'll be in touch.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks if maintenance is hiring; the janitor says they're always looking for the next generation
jokes.punchline: 'Throw your resume away' — the advice is to literally discard the resume as the application process, implying the job requires zero credentials
jokes.explanation: Clean deadpan. 'Throw your resume away' as the application instruction is a sharp little joke about the hierarchy of employment — the janitor's job requires you to shed ambition rather than demonstrate it. The 'fourth floor' specificity is good comic detail.

jokes.text: The updated title tagline at the table read: 'Pride Pad. Pride: The World Is Your Toilet.' (revised from the earlier 'Make Every Room a Bathroom')
jokes.setup: The bladder pad sponsor was previously introduced with a slightly more restrained tagline
jokes.punchline: 'The World Is Your Toilet' — a philosophical escalation of the earlier tagline, even more brazenly undignified
jokes.explanation: Works as a running gag with escalation — 'Make Every Room a Bathroom' was funny; 'The World Is Your Toilet' takes the same joke further in a different direction. Both are parodies of the inspirational ad-copy voice applied to incontinence. The callback structure adds value.

jokes.text: The table read screenplay description: 'We smash cut to a night of passion in a completely dark room. Bathing suit areas get a workout.'
jokes.setup: Liz is reading her screenplay at a table read as if it's a normal romantic scene
jokes.punchline: 'Bathing suit areas get a workout' — a hilariously clinical/prudish euphemism for sex, characteristic of Liz Lemon's voice
jokes.explanation: 'Bathing suit areas' is quintessential Liz Lemon — her sexuality is perpetually filtered through an adolescent awkwardness. The phrase 'get a workout' adds a fitness-class register that makes it even funnier. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: The screenplay stage direction description of Liz's character: 'Jack's friend Liz — think Courteney Cox — dances with a handsome pilot — think a young Fred Grandy.'
jokes.setup: The screenplay describes its characters with 'think [famous actor]' shorthand
jokes.punchline: Liz's flattering self-comparison to Courteney Cox is immediately undercut by the pilot being 'a young Fred Grandy' — the Gopher from The Love Boat, not exactly a romantic ideal
jokes.explanation: The pairing of Courteney Cox (aspirational but not outrageous) with Fred Grandy (a deep-cut Love Boat reference, not glamorous) is the joke. Liz's self-mythologizing alongside her taste in men is perfectly in character. Requires pop-culture awareness for full effect.

jokes.text: Nancy's Boston accent and line: '[ridiculous Boston accent] Jack, who's calling ya at such a wicked late hour? Ya mother?'
jokes.setup: The screenplay describes Nancy as Jack's high school sweetheart
jokes.punchline: The over-the-top Boston accent ('wicked late hour, ya mother') played for comedic exaggeration
jokes.explanation: The accent gag is somewhat broad and familiar — 'wicked' Boston accent jokes are common. It works because the transcript calls it 'ridiculous' and the show has established this as an ongoing bit, but it doesn't rise above functional.

jokes.text: The unnamed man's come-on to Liz: 'I got four inches of steel that might change your mind.' (after she says he's married to a woman)
jokes.setup: Liz compliments a man on his skin; he says he's married to a woman (implying gay); Liz still finds him attractive
jokes.punchline: His double-entendre — 'four inches of steel' — is either a wedding ring reference or a crude sexual boast, deliberately ambiguous
jokes.explanation: The setup is more interesting than the punchline. The ambiguity of 'four inches of steel' (a ring? a threat?) is mildly clever but the joke relies on innuendo more than wit. Functional but not sharp.

jokes.text: Jack: 'I turned down intercourse with Harvey Weinstein on no less than three occasions... out of five.'
jokes.setup: Jack boasts he's not afraid of anyone in show business
jokes.punchline: 'Out of five' — the qualifier transforms a boast into a confession that he accepted on two occasions
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: the initial statement ('on no less than three occasions') reads as a boast of virtue; 'out of five' is a tiny two-word clause that retroactively makes it a confession and reveals exactly how much of Jack's willpower was involved. Maximum information in minimum words. Also a sharp Hollywood power satire. The timing pause implied by '...' before 'out of five' is the punchline delivery. Extremely quotable. Note: given subsequent real-world events concerning Weinstein, this joke has gained an uncomfortable additional resonance, but in isolation the construction is excellent.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'What do you think Phil Collins was trying to do with Sussudio?' / Jenna: 'Which Weird Al famously parodied with Soup Soupy-o.'
jokes.setup: Tracy claims it's impossible to write a Weird Al-proof song, citing Phil Collins as an example
jokes.punchline: 'Soup Soupy-o' — the made-up Weird Al parody title for Sussudio is funny because it sounds plausible and ridiculous simultaneously
jokes.explanation: 'Soup Soupy-o' is excellent — it follows the exact logic of a Weird Al parody (substitute a nonsense food item, keep the phonetics). It sounds like it could be real, which is the joke's greatest strength. Good absurdist construction.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'I'll make coffee. You also make coffee. After the coffee contest, we'll start working.'
jokes.setup: The group is gearing up to solve the Weird Al problem
jokes.punchline: Tracy immediately derails into a coffee competition — the non-sequitur reveals that Tracy's priorities are always elsewhere
jokes.explanation: Reliable Tracy — his process for solving any problem involves an immediate side-tangent that has nothing to do with the task. 'Coffee contest' as a way of not working is a good Tracy bit.

jokes.text: Jack complains that Liz twisted the facts 'like Chubby Checker took the traditional standing dance and made a mockery of it with The Twist.'
jokes.setup: Jack is upset that Liz included the Nancy subplot in the screenplay
jokes.punchline: Jack's characterization of The Twist as a subversion/mockery of 'the traditional standing dance' reveals his conservative sensibility applied to something absurd
jokes.explanation: Peak Jack Donaghy. The joke is him deploying the simile with complete sincerity — 'the traditional standing dance' is not a phrase anyone has ever used before, and his genuine indignation at The Twist's disruption of it is perfect. The comedy is entirely in Jack's worldview being applied to something ridiculous.

jokes.text: Liz: 'You wouldn't say that if you read my MythBusters fan fiction. It is sexy. And you're welcome.'
jokes.setup: Jack says Liz has no idea how to write romance
jokes.punchline: Liz's evidence of her romantic writing ability is MythBusters erotic fan fiction — specific enough to be perfect
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific joke. MythBusters fan fiction is perfect because it's specific enough to be real (MythBusters fan fiction genuinely exists), unexpected enough to be absurd, and exactly right for Liz — a nerdy, food-and-TV-obsessed woman who would channel sexuality into genre shows. 'And you're welcome' is a great addition, implying she's conferring a gift on the world. High quotability.

jokes.text: Diana Jessup's entrance line to Liz: 'I'm glad to see the endgame of feminism is women dressing like Dennis the Menace at work.'
jokes.setup: Diana, a patrician WASP, meets Liz for the first time
jokes.punchline: 'Dennis the Menace' as a specific description of Liz's style — the cartoon-character comparison is specific, mean, and accurate
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest lines in the episode. 'The endgame of feminism is women dressing like Dennis the Menace at work' works on two levels: it's an aristocratic put-down of both Liz's fashion and feminist politics, and it's a pitch-perfect description of how Liz actually dresses. The specificity of 'Dennis the Menace' (not just 'a child') is what makes it land — it conjures a very specific striped-sweater, disheveled visual. Excellent introduction of Diana's character in one line.

jokes.text: Diana: 'Because it's crass, Jack. Like personalized wedding vows or standing up in a pool.'
jokes.setup: Diana explains why the TV movie is inappropriate
jokes.punchline: Her examples of 'crass' — personalized vows and standing in a pool — reveal her aristocratic code of conduct: informal = vulgar
jokes.explanation: A genuinely great character joke. 'Personalized wedding vows' as crass is recognizable upper-class snobbery, but 'standing up in a pool' is the unexpected second example that makes the joke. Nobody says 'standing up in a pool' is crass — the implication is that one should float or sit in pools, never stand, and this absurd specificity reveals Diana's world perfectly. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Diana: 'To hear about it the way I did. My housekeeper started screaming.'
jokes.setup: Diana explains how she heard about the TV movie
jokes.punchline: The image of a housekeeper screaming as her method of news delivery is absurd — implying a chaotic, dramatic response to what seems like minor news
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist beat. The screaming housekeeper implies Diana inhabits a world where dramatic reactions to minor events are normal, or conversely that the housekeeper is deeply invested in celebrity news. Either reading is funny.

jokes.text: Diana: 'And I didn't dream that I was a sex slave to a squid-like alien with your head.'
jokes.setup: Diana and Jack are performing an elaborate dance of denial about their mutual attraction
jokes.punchline: Diana volunteers an extremely specific dream — a squid-alien with Jack's head — as proof that nothing is awkward between them, which achieves the opposite
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The construction is perfect: Diana is denying awkwardness by bringing up a dream that proves the opposite, and the dream itself — sex slave to a squid-alien with Jack's head — is so specific and so deranged that it becomes its own comedic object. 'Squid-like' is the perfect qualifier. The joke works on three levels: the irony of denial-as-confession, the absurdist imagery, and the insight into Diana's repression. One of the episode's absolute best.

jokes.text: Jack: 'I'd love to have you. Uh, I mean, as a guest, not, uh, under a waterfall.'
jokes.setup: Jack tells Diana he'd love to have her stay — classic social pleasantry
jokes.punchline: He corrects himself by specifying 'not under a waterfall' — implying that thought was present enough to need exclusion
jokes.explanation: 'Under a waterfall' as the specific forbidden scenario is a great choice — it implies Jack has a particular fantasy and is suppressing it poorly. The self-correction technique (where a character's denial reveals exactly what they're denying) is a reliable cringe structure, but executed here with atypical specificity.

jokes.text: Diana: 'The train was disgusting.' [exits] [beat] 'I flew here, but I saw a train from the window.'
jokes.setup: Diana exits saying the train was disgusting — a normal complaint
jokes.punchline: She returns to clarify she actually flew; she just saw a train. The complaint about the train's condition is hearsay from a window.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: an innocuous exit line, a pause, and then a return to clarify information that makes the original complaint completely absurd. The comedy is in Diana's need to be accurate about a complaint that no longer applies to her — she flew, but still wants credit for observing that trains are disgusting. It's a precise character joke: she's snobbish, she's fastidious, and she cannot let an imprecise statement stand. Extremely economical and highly quotable.

jokes.text: Jack's reaction: 'What are you doing? Leave.' / Liz: 'No. This is weird and I am not letting it get any weirder. All my life, I have been the third wheel that prevents people from having sex.'
jokes.setup: Jack wants Liz to leave so he can be alone with Diana
jokes.punchline: Liz reveals her self-appointed social function: professional sexual cockblocker. She frames it as heroism.
jokes.explanation: 'Third wheel that prevents people from having sex' is a specific and funny self-definition. The joke is that Liz is proud of this role, which tells us everything about her character. Sets up 'the blocker' running gag.

jokes.text: Liz: 'I'm sorry, but you're stressed and you're lonely and that woman has flawless skin, like an organic chicken. I haven't had lunch.'
jokes.setup: Liz is defending her decision to stay and chaperone
jokes.punchline: 'Like an organic chicken. I haven't had lunch.' — the skin compliment immediately triggers a food association, and Liz admits it in the same breath
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Liz Lemon moment. The simile 'flawless skin, like an organic chicken' is inspired — it's simultaneously a genuine compliment (smooth, pale) and a deranged food metaphor, and then Liz immediately breaks to admit she's hungry. The non-sequitur is perfectly earned: Liz's brain is never far from food, and the skin-to-chicken association is exactly how her mind works. Very quotable, strong character integration.

jokes.text: Kenneth's janitor interview speech: '...only small people, like children, or a giant who's very far away from you.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth delivers an earnest inspirational speech about there being no small jobs
jokes.punchline: His illustration of 'small people' includes not just children but 'a giant who's very far away from you' — a literal-minded addition that demolishes the inspirational rhetoric
jokes.explanation: Kenneth at his finest. The joke is that he's earnestly trying to make a metaphor work but his literalist brain can't help adding 'or a giant who's very far away from you' — which is technically correct but completely undermines the inspirational force. It reveals Kenneth's guileless, hyper-literal worldview perfectly. High quotability and character specificity.

jokes.text: Kenneth sings the NBC jingle ('I love this') during his pitch to get his job back.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is making an earnest case to return to NBC
jokes.punchline: He breaks into the actual NBC jingle as evidence of his loyalty — deeply sincere, completely unironic
jokes.explanation: Meta and sweet — Kenneth's pathological devotion to NBC expressed through the jingle is a recurring character element. Less funny on its own than as part of the Kenneth mythology.

jokes.text: Liz interrupts the fitting with STD statistics: 'One in four Americans has an STD. Chlamydia, herpes, garden variety genital swelling—' / Jack: 'That's quite enough, Lemon.' / Liz: 'Rectal fissures.'
jokes.setup: Liz has announced she 'likes factoids' and begins sharing one
jokes.punchline: She continues past Jack's attempt to stop her, adding 'rectal fissures' as the final overshare
jokes.explanation: The joke is structured as escalating discomfort with a button — 'rectal fissures' is the perfect final term because it's the most clinical and specific and crosses a clear line. The pause after Jack's 'that's quite enough' gives the punchline room. The setup is Liz's inability to read the social situation. Good structure.

jokes.text: Lance Drake Mandrell introducing himself as 'method acting, staying in character at all times. It's a technique invented by Constantin Stanislavski when he was four years old and wanted to act like a pirate.'
jokes.setup: Lance announces he'll be method acting to play Jack
jokes.punchline: His citation of Stanislavski's origin story — a four-year-old wanting to be a pirate — is completely fabricated and absurd, delivered with total confidence
jokes.explanation: The fake actor history is a good bit — it simultaneously satirizes method acting pretension and the kind of actor who confidently mangles facts. 'Four years old and wanted to act like a pirate' is a very specific absurdist image.

jokes.text: Lance to Diana: 'Diana, are you a time-traveler? Because I don't know how my mother-in-law could be younger than my wife.'
jokes.setup: Lance meets Diana and deploys a practiced compliment
jokes.punchline: The time-travel framing for an age-based compliment is both cheesy and somewhat charming — the joke is Lance's actor-brained way of flattering
jokes.explanation: The time-traveler pickup line is a well-worn compliment format, but it works here because Lance is clearly an actor deploying a scripted charm offensive. The setup 'I don't know how my mother-in-law could be younger than my wife' is a solid phrasing. Functional.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Was that supposed to be me saying that? Because I would never use that much math in complimenting a woman. Their brains can't handle it.'
jokes.setup: Lance has just delivered a compliment involving a time-travel math-adjacent observation
jokes.punchline: Jack's objection is not to the sexism but to the perceived over-complexity — his dismissal of women's mathematical capacity is delivered as a known fact, revealing his unreconstructed worldview
jokes.explanation: Sharp Jack character comedy. His objection to the compliment's use of 'math' (time travel is not really math) as cognitively overwhelming to women is a perfect encapsulation of his patrician, sexist worldview. The specificity ('that much math') implies there is an acceptable quantity of math for women, just not this much. Diana's giggle and 'it's evolution' response is a funny capper.

jokes.text: Lance: 'Hey, quick question, Jack. Our underwear, is it regular black bikini cut? Or is it silk boxers with Tweety Bird on them? Because I have both.'
jokes.setup: Lance is method acting as Jack and inquiring about character details
jokes.punchline: The method actor's research question concerns underwear, and the options are 'regular black bikini cut' vs. 'silk boxers with Tweety Bird on them' — neither of which is obviously correct for Jack
jokes.explanation: The method actor absurdism is good — the specificity of the two options (one dignified, one ridiculous) captures Lance's complete inability to inhabit Jack's character. 'Tweety Bird on them' is a great comic detail. Also implies Lance personally owns Tweety Bird boxers.

jokes.text: Diana's description of Lance/Jack: 'The fighter pilot wrists, the hair like a mature otter's pelt, shoulders you could ride bareback.'
jokes.setup: Diana is observing Lance's resemblance to Jack
jokes.punchline: Her physical descriptions escalate in sensuality and animal metaphor — 'mature otter's pelt' for hair and 'ride bareback' for shoulders are genuinely strange and revealing of her attraction
jokes.explanation: Exceptional writing. 'A mature otter's pelt' is a bizarre and specific simile that is funny because it's simultaneously accurate as a hair texture description and wildly animalistic. 'Ride bareback' is overtly sexual and Diana delivers it with the affect of someone describing a mountain vista. The three-part escalation structure (wrists → hair → shoulders) works perfectly. Very quotable, perfect character integration.

jokes.text: The wardrobe coordinator to Diana about Lance: 'Every woman here would love to slip it to your son-in-law... Drill him against a wall... Give him the old skin flute.'
jokes.setup: The wardrobe person is explaining to Diana that Jack is attractive
jokes.punchline: Each successive euphemism for sex gets cruder, with the person clearly not reading the room; 'skin flute' is the final escalation
jokes.explanation: The escalation works reasonably well — each phrase is more explicit than the last. 'Skin flute' is an unusual slang term that adds to the comedy through its unexpectedness. But the joke is mostly just crude escalation without a sharp punchline beyond the delivery to Diana.

jokes.text: Tracy rejects 'these lonely eyes' by instantly hearing 'baloney thighs': 'I'm sorry, did you just say baloney thighs? Because that's the name of the boat Weird Al's gonna buy with the money he makes off you... dumb bitch! I'm sorry. I just care too much.'
jokes.setup: Jenna tries another lyric ('these lonely eyes')
jokes.punchline: Tracy mishears/re-parodies it as 'baloney thighs,' names the boat, calls her a 'dumb bitch,' then immediately apologizes out of 'caring too much' — the emotional pivot is the capper
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tracy moment. 'Baloney thighs' is the perfect stupid parody title. Naming the boat Weird Al will buy adds a vivid specific detail. The profanity followed by 'I just care too much' is a perfect Tracy emotional logic — he insults out of love. Very quotable, strong character integration.

jokes.text: The pizza song epiphany: 'We might as well just write a song about pizza... Oh, my god. If we did that, he'd be powerless. There's nothing you can change pizza to.' / Tracy: 'Because it's already weird.' / Jenna: 'Exactly. Weird Al's about to get a taste of his own medicine.'
jokes.setup: The characters are frustrated that every song can be parodied
jokes.punchline: The logical conclusion — write a song ABOUT pizza, which is already too absurd to parody — is presented as a stroke of genius
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly constructed absurdist logic. The insight that pizza is 'already weird' — too absurd to be made more absurd by Weird Al — is a genuinely funny comedic premise that has its own internal logic. The payoff when Jenna actually performs the pizza song on Fallon is earned. 'Weird Al's about to get a taste of his own medicine' is a perfect straight-faced delivery of a ridiculous conclusion.

jokes.text: Lance practicing being Jack: 'I'm Jack Donaghy.' [pause] 'I am Jack Donaghy.' [retches] 'Oh, god. This iced tea is so strong.'
jokes.setup: Lance is rehearsing his role as Jack by repeatedly stating Jack's name
jokes.punchline: He starts gagging — seemingly from the effort of becoming Jack or from alcohol in what he thought was iced tea
jokes.explanation: The 'iced tea' reveal (implying it's actually alcohol) is a nice understated runner. The repetition of 'I'm Jack Donaghy / I am Jack Donaghy' as the extent of method acting preparation is funny in its banality.

jokes.text: Diana: 'Rose wine?' / Lance: 'Pairs well with failed suicide.'
jokes.setup: Lance is performing as Jack; Diana offers wine
jokes.punchline: 'Pairs well with failed suicide' — Lance/Jack's wine pairing recommendation is pitch-black and completely unexpected
jokes.explanation: Dark and economical. The wine pairing format is familiar (pairs well with X), but 'failed suicide' as X is unexpected and blackly funny. Diana's 'Oh!' response implies this is also correct for Jack — it reveals something about his character. Very quotable, tight structure.

jokes.text: Lance, staying in character as Jack: 'There hasn't been a good non-boat painting in 5,000 years.'
jokes.setup: Liz tries to leave; Lance stays in character to keep her there
jokes.punchline: 'There hasn't been a good non-boat painting in 5,000 years' — a perfectly Jack-like confident aesthetic pronouncement that is both plausible and absurd
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Lance-as-Jack jokes. The statement sounds like something Jack would absolutely say — authoritative, specific, historically sweeping, aesthetically conservative. 'Non-boat painting' is a beautiful invention of a category. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Liz's voice-over/realization: 'Sometimes to prevent monkey business, we must create it. The blocker.'
jokes.setup: Liz has just orchestrated getting Diana and Lance together
jokes.punchline: She names herself 'The Blocker' with apparent pride as if it's a superhero identity
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback that formalizes Liz's self-appointed role. The aphorism ('to prevent monkey business, we must create it') is funny in its self-serious framing. Works as character comedy payoff.

jokes.text: Lance to Jack: 'How is taking your mother-in-law out on a date acting like you?' / Jack: 'Uh, it's not, obviously.'
jokes.setup: Jack tells Lance to 'stop acting like me' after Lance invites Diana for a drink
jokes.punchline: Lance points out that taking his mother-in-law on a date IS something Jack would do — Jack's flustered non-denial confirms it
jokes.explanation: A well-structured irony beat. The joke is that Lance, by method acting as Jack, has arrived at the same behavior Jack has been suppressing. Jack's 'Uh, it's not, obviously' is a telltale non-denial.

jokes.text: Diana: 'It's impossible not to have a great time at Planet Hollywood.'
jokes.setup: Diana tells Jack she and Lance will have a great time on their date
jokes.punchline: Planet Hollywood — a dated, tacky celebrity-themed chain restaurant — as Diana Jessup's idea of a great date venue is an absurd class collision
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the specific venue choice. Diana, who found 'standing in a pool' crass, has chosen Planet Hollywood — one of the tackiest chain restaurants imaginable. Either it's a character inconsistency played for laughs, or she's doing it to scandalize Jack. Either reading is funny. The deadpan delivery amplifies it.

jokes.text: Jack's confrontation with Liz: 'An idea that's off the charts, kemosabe.'
jokes.setup: Jack is workshopping catch-phrases for himself in the screenplay
jokes.punchline: 'Kemosabe' — Lone Ranger's term of address — tacked onto what is already a bland corporate-speak phrase, revealing Jack's total tin ear for colloquial speech
jokes.explanation: 'Kemosabe' is a bizarre and specific choice that Jack deploys with complete earnestness. It becomes a callback later when it appears in the actual movie, which pays off the joke. The combination of hollow corporate enthusiasm and frontier slang is very Jack.

jokes.text: Jack's table read script: 'I've never been kissed like that, Jack.' / 'It's because we're so in love, Avery. That's why we're perfect, Avery.' / 'Make love to me... Now.' [Jack: 'This is garbage.']
jokes.setup: Jack has fired Liz and decided to write the movie himself; he reads what he's written
jokes.punchline: His draft is embarrassingly basic romantic cliché ('we're so in love,' 'that's why we're perfect') and he immediately realizes it — 'this is garbage'
jokes.explanation: The comedy is Jack's lack of self-awareness — he fires the writer and produces something much worse. The reading of his own horrible dialogue followed by 'this is garbage' is a clean self-own. The script's repetition of 'Avery' in consecutive sentences is a nice touch of badness.

jokes.text: Kenneth, dressed as a janitor, is asked 'Why are you dressed like a janitor?' / 'It's my new job.' / 'But you just got promoted.' / Kenneth explains: 'Not the dream where those two tennis sisters chase me.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth mentions his 'career dreams' as distinct from other dreams
jokes.punchline: 'Not the dream where those two tennis sisters chase me' — the specific clarification reveals a recurring nightmare about the Williams sisters
jokes.explanation: The qualifier 'not the dream where those two tennis sisters chase me' is excellent Kenneth — he disambiguates between his dreams with the same earnestness he gives to everything. The specificity of 'the two tennis sisters' (clearly the Williams sisters) and the fact that it's a recurring dream creates an absurd secondary character mythology in one clause. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Jack's speech to Kenneth conflates their situations: 'Even if other people say to you, your life is a mess. Stop looking at your mother-in-law. I can't write your movie.'
jokes.setup: Jack is supposedly giving Kenneth an inspirational speech about resilience
jokes.punchline: The advice is transparently about Jack's own problems — 'stop looking at your mother-in-law, I can't write your movie' has nothing to do with Kenneth
jokes.explanation: The projection joke works well — Jack is obviously not talking to Kenneth but to himself, and the specificity of 'stop looking at your mother-in-law' as general life advice is funny. Kenneth's earnest reception of this bizarre advice makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Kenneth's secret: '[whispers] I lie to myself. Every morning, when I wake up, I say, everything's gonna be okay. But I'm lying. And I don't know how much longer I can do it.' [piercing inhalation] 'Have a swell night, sir.'
jokes.setup: Jack asks how Kenneth stays positive
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's confession of systematic self-deception — followed by a devastated pause and a cheerful 'have a swell night' — is the darkest and most vulnerable Kenneth moment in the episode
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the great Kenneth moments in the series. The confession is structured perfectly: the whispered setup, the devastating admission, the pause ('I don't know how much longer I can do it'), and then the immediate pivot to 'have a swell night, sir' — snapping back to the Kenneth persona as if the curtain never parted. It works as comedy (the contrast between the confession and the exit line) and as genuinely moving character work. The 'piercing inhalation' detail suggests a barely suppressed breakdown. Extremely quotable. Touches something true about performing happiness.

jokes.text: Jenna after the Fallon performance: 'Let me guess, you're all watching my triumph on Fallon last night?'
jokes.setup: Jenna enters to find people watching something on a screen
jokes.punchline: She assumes it's her triumph — revealing Jenna's reflexive narcissism — but they're watching something else
jokes.explanation: Reliable Jenna-narcissism beat. The word 'triumph' is a nice self-aggrandizing touch for a pizza fart song performance.

jokes.text: Normal Al's parody: Weird Al reverses the parody strategy, turning Jenna's pizza fart song into a touching song about a soldier returning home.
jokes.setup: Jenna's pizza song was designed to be Weird-Al-proof because 'it's already weird'
jokes.punchline: Weird Al out-maneuvers them by de-weirding the song — 'He normal Al'd us' — turning fart jokes into patriotic sentiment
jokes.explanation: Exceptional payoff to the episode's absurdist subplot. The invention of 'Normal Al' as a concept — Weird Al doing the opposite of parody, making weird things sincere — is a genuinely original comedic idea. 'He normal Al'd us' is an instant classic phrase. The structure is perfect: the plan that was too clever is defeated by an even cleverer reversal. Tracy's devastated 'Yankovic!' and Jenna's genuine emotion ('I've gotta go call my dad') add character resonance. Arguably the episode's funniest concept.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Everyone lies to themselves. I mean, I refuse to buy larger underwear, and it looks like when you tie a string around a roast.'
jokes.setup: Liz is telling Jack that everyone lies to themselves, using herself as an example
jokes.punchline: 'It looks like when you tie a string around a roast' — the specific cooking metaphor applied to underwear-muffin-top is unexpected and grotesque
jokes.explanation: Excellent Liz self-deprecation. The specific image of underwear cutting into flesh 'like when you tie a string around a roast' is visually precise, unexpected, and perfectly Liz — she finds cooking metaphors for her body. The image is so specific it becomes unforgettable. Strong character integration and high quotability.

jokes.text: The movie's climax: 'I'll never let you capture my wife from here, on the top of the Empire State Building!' / 'Korean freeze ray!' / 'Jack!' / 'Nothing can keep us apart! Our love is off the charts, kemosabe.'
jokes.setup: The TV movie being filmed is reaching its climax
jokes.punchline: 'Korean freeze ray' and 'our love is off the charts, kemosabe' — the movie has fully embraced the absurd version of events, and Jack's terrible catchphrase is now canon
jokes.explanation: The callback of 'kemosabe' in the actual movie dialogue is a satisfying payoff. 'Korean freeze ray' is a good absurdist movie-villain device. The Empire State Building setting also parodies King Kong/romantic movie conventions.

jokes.text: Lance's debriefing about Diana: 'She's a real hotshot at boinking. She boinks like a dog. I'm not a writer. She made me boink her this morning and at first, I was like, please—'
jokes.setup: Lance is thanking Jack and updating him on Diana
jokes.punchline: Lance's elaborate, graceless, overly detailed sexual report to his subject's son-in-law, using 'boink' repeatedly and adding 'like a dog' as a simile
jokes.explanation: The cringe escalates with each use of 'boink' — it's a deliberately childish word used in an adult context, which increases the awkwardness. 'I'm not a writer' (explaining why 'like a dog' is his best simile) is a perfect self-aware disclaimer that also echoes earlier self-deprecating 'I'm not a writer' moments. Jack's increasingly pained face is inferred.

jokes.text: Lance: 'Get back to doing the things I love, like getting high and going to the planetarium.'
jokes.setup: Lance is relieved to be done with the project
jokes.punchline: His two listed loves — getting high and the planetarium — are a perfect actor-dude pairing
jokes.explanation: The pairing of weed and the planetarium is a clean joke — stoner + stars is a coherent universe, but stating them as equal life passions gives Lance a lovely, specific personality. Good economy.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Hey, when this movie airs, can my name be the first credit that comes up at the end?' / Jack: 'This is a group process, Lemon. Don't be an egomaniac.'
jokes.setup: Liz and Jack have just resolved their conflict and the movie is done
jokes.punchline: Liz's petty request — first credit at the end (the least prestigious position) — is called out as egomaniacal by Jack, who has been the actual egomaniac the entire episode
jokes.explanation: A good closing beat. Jack calling Liz an egomaniac for wanting the end credits is a perfect ironic cap after an episode of his own narcissism. 'First credit that comes up at the end' is itself funny — it's both specific and a relatively minor vanity.

tmdb_overview: Liz's scripted version of Jack and Avery's love story leaves Jack confused and frustrated by his feelings for Diana. Meanwhile, Jenna and Tracy attempt to beat Weird Al Yankovic at his own game, and Kenneth gets an unexpected new job at NBC.
insight: Absurdist character comedy sustains 61 jokes across 42 minutes despite middling impact scores.
